paras: The lynching of Charles Diddell was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a bridge at Weston, Platte County, Missouri, on the evening of Sunday, June 12, 1881. Diddell, whose name was also printed "Didell," had been jailed that day, accused of raping and trying to kill a young white woman, and the mob took him from the jail and hanged him without trial. Papers from Chicago to Savannah carried the story; one wire brief named the victim "Ruse" and said his head was cut off after the hanging.

The accuser was named as Nancy Stillwell by the Chicago Tribune, "Annie Stillwater" by the Richmond Democrat and "Nannie Stillwell" by the Lexington Weekly Intelligencer, and her age was given as 19 or 16. According to the Richmond Democrat, she was walking in the woods near her father's house that Sunday when she was attacked. The reports charged that her attacker raped her and then tried to kill her, the Tribune saying he left her "for dead with a crushed skull" and the Richmond paper that he cut her throat and beat her head with a club. She was said to be alive at last accounts, though the Richmond Democrat reported she was not expected to live.

Townspeople pursued the accused man, and the Hermanner Volksblatt, a German-language Missouri weekly, reported that he was found in an abandoned farmhouse with blood on his clothes and taken back to the Weston jail. Several papers said he confessed: the Tribune that he "admitted the crime" when arrested, the Volksblatt that he confessed between 5 and 6 p.m., and the Southern Standard of McMinnville, Tennessee, that he was "forced to confess." Meanwhile, the Volksblatt wrote, people from the surrounding country filled the streets, and about 8 p.m. a deputation demanded the prisoner at the jail.

The guards refused but were overpowered, and the prisoner, bound hand and foot, passed to what the paper called the merciless crowd. The Richmond Democrat described the lynchers as "a party of armed men," and the Tribune's dispatch said a mob took him "from the Sheriff." He was taken to a bridge, "a high bridge" in the Tribune and "the Railroad bridge" in the Richmond Democrat, where a rope around his neck was tied to a beam. Asked whether he had more to say, he answered, by the Volksblatt's account, that he regretted the deed and knew he deserved death. A brother of the young woman then pushed him off, according to the Tribune; the Volksblatt said her brothers did so, and the Southern Standard that her brother adjusted the noose.
The Kansas City dispatch said the coroner cut the body down the next morning. No report of an inquest verdict, arrests or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The first report was a Kansas City dispatch of June 13, printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune on June 14 under the deck "A Negro at Weston, Mo., Taken from the Sheriff and Lynched." Fuller Missouri versions followed in the Richmond Democrat (June 16), the Hermanner Volksblatt (June 17) and the Lexington Weekly Intelligencer (June 18). These papers treated the accusation as established; the Richmond Democrat said "The brute met a just fate," while the Volksblatt called him a beast in human form yet called the crowd merciless.

A separate wire brief, printed on June 17 in The Daily Gazette and the Daily Republican and on June 20 in the Savannah Morning News, named the victim only as "a colored man named Ruse" and added that his head was cut off and thrown into the Missouri River. Later in June a news brief in Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies treated the hanging lightly as one of "Two neck-tie sociables," calling Diddell "a negro rapist" and placing Weston in Nebraska.

Every account but the Ruse brief names the victim Diddell or Didell, and the Ruse brief's "Tuesday night" cannot be squared with a June 13 dispatch already reporting the lynching, which the Missouri papers place on Sunday evening. The beheading also rests on that brief alone; the Lexington paper said the body was cast into a stream, the Tribune that the coroner cut it down.

accounts.label: Kansas City dispatch
accounts.gist: Diddell, who had admitted the crime when arrested, was taken by a mob from the Sheriff late at night to a high bridge and pushed off by the girl's brother; the Coroner cut down the body in the morning.

accounts.label: Missouri papers
accounts.gist: The assault took place Sunday in the woods near the girl's home; the accused was captured, jailed at Weston and confessed, and about 8 p.m. armed men or a deputation backed by a crowd took him from the jail and hanged him from a (railroad) bridge.

accounts.label: 'Ruse' wire brief
accounts.gist: A colored man named Ruse was taken from the Weston jail on Tuesday night and lynched; after the hanging his head was cut off and thrown into the Missouri River.

framing.detail: The Chicago Tribune headed the dispatch 'A Negro Lynched', called the charge 'a nameless crime' and said the brother 'pushed him into eternity', without comment on the mob.
The Richmond Democrat called the accused 'the brute' and said he 'met a just fate and retribution was none too soon'.
The Hermanner Volksblatt called the accused a 'Bestie' (beast) in human form but called the crowd that seized him merciless ('erbarmungslosen').
The 'Ruse' brief ran in general-news columns with no comment beyond the beheading detail.
Minnesota and Wisconsin weeklies made light of it as one of 'Two neck-tie sociables' and called the victim 'a negro rapist'.

conflicts.note: Every account except the one wire brief gives Diddell/Didell, including the earliest dispatch and three Missouri papers.
